1.s: God calls young Jeremiah: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you.” Jeremiah protests he is only a youth, but God touches his mouth and shows him an almond branch and a boiling pot.
1.d: Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah from Anathoth, was called in the 13th year of King Josiah [[tbd:010:Jeremiah (Person)]] [[bible:Jeremiah 1:1-2]]. The Hebrew words for “almond tree” (shaqed) and “watching” (shoqed) sound alike: God is watching over his word [[tosn:Jeremiah 1:11–12]].

2.s: God remembers Israel’s first love, but they have forsaken him, “the spring of living waters”, for broken cisterns.
2.d: Jeremiah uses marriage, infidelity and divorce as pictures of Judah’s spiritual betrayal [[tosn:Jeremiah 2:1–13]]. A spring that flows all year, even in drought, is a rare treasure [[tosn:Jeremiah 2:13]] [[bible:John 4:14]].

3.s: Faithless Israel and treacherous Judah are called to return: “Return, you backsliding children, and I will heal your backsliding.”
3.d: Judah committed spiritual adultery, assuming God would not object [[tosn:Jeremiah 3:1–5]]. God promises shepherds who will guide with knowledge and understanding [[tosn:Jeremiah 3:15]].

4.s: A call to circumcise the heart, then a vision of invasion from the north: the earth “waste and void”, as before creation.
4.d: The call to circumcise the heart means giving up the pride and power the people prized [[tosn:Jeremiah 4:4]]. In 4:23–26 God’s judgement reverses the order of creation (compare Genesis 1:2) [[tosn:Jeremiah 4:23–26]].

5.s: Search Jerusalem for one person who does justice. The people refuse correction; prophets and priests lie.
5.d: Jeremiah searched for anyone who acted justly and spoke truthfully, and found neither [[tosn:Jeremiah 5:1–2]]. The people had working eyes and ears but stubbornly ignored what they saw and heard [[tosn:Jeremiah 5:20–21]] [[bible:Mark 8:18]].

6.s: Jerusalem is besieged; they say “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace. “Ask for the old paths… and walk in it.”
6.d: The invasion from the north, likely the Babylonians in 605 BC, was approaching, and Jeremiah had to warn the people [[tosn:Jeremiah 6:1–9]]. The “old paths” bring rest for the soul (compare Matthew 11:29) [[tosn:Jeremiah 6:16]].

7.s: At the temple gate Jeremiah says not to trust in “Yahweh’s temple”; God will destroy it as he did Shiloh if they do not change their ways.
7.d: Jesus quotes “a den of robbers” when he clears the temple [[tosn:Jeremiah 7:11]] [[bible:Matthew 21:13]]. The valley of Ben-Hinnom, where children were sacrificed, is called Gehenna in the New Testament [[tosn:Jeremiah 7:30–34]].

8.s: The people do not repent. “The harvest is past, the summer has ended, and we are not saved.” “Is there no balm in Gilead?”
8.d: The balm of Gilead was a resin from trees east of the Jordan, sold for its healing power [[tosn:Jeremiah 8:22]]. The African-American spiritual “There Is a Balm in Gilead” names Jesus as the true healer [[tosn:Jeremiah 8:22]].

9.s: Jeremiah wishes his head were a fountain of tears. “let him who glories glory in this, that he has understanding, and knows me”
9.d: Professional mourners performed at funerals in the ancient Near East [[tosn:Jeremiah 9:17]]. The only boast God values is knowing him, which Paul quotes in 1 Corinthians 1:31 [[tosn:Jeremiah 9:24]].

10.s: Idols are like scarecrows in a cucumber field; the living God made the earth by his power.
10.d: A poem mocking idols and praising the one true God [[tosn:Jeremiah 10:1–16]]. Verse 11 is written in Aramaic, perhaps a saying aimed at Babylon, where Aramaic was spoken [[tosn:Jeremiah 10:11]].

11.s: The people have broken the covenant. Jeremiah learns of a plot against his life by his own townspeople.
11.d: Jeremiah brings God’s covenant charges against Judah [[tosn:Jeremiah 11:1–3]]. Some scholars see the gentle lamb of 11:19 as foreshadowing Christ, like the servant of Isaiah 53:7 [[tosn:Jeremiah 11:18–19]].

12.s: Jeremiah asks why the wicked prosper; God answers that harder trials are coming.
12.d: Jeremiah asks why a just God does not quickly punish the wicked [[tosn:Jeremiah 12:1–4]]. A vineyard often stands for God’s people (Isaiah 5; John 15) [[tosn:Jeremiah 12:10]].

13.s: Jeremiah buries a linen belt until it is ruined: so God will ruin Judah’s pride. “Can the Ethiopian change his skin?”
13.d: The linen loincloth is an acted parable of Judah’s unrighteousness [[tosn:Jeremiah 13:1–2]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 13:1–14]]. God had bound his people to himself for his renown [[tosn:Jeremiah 13:10–11]].

14.s: In a drought Jeremiah prays for the people, but God says not to pray for them, and false prophets promise peace.
14.d: A conversation between God, Jeremiah and the people, begun by a severe drought [[tosn:Jeremiah 14:1–22]].

15.s: Even Moses and Samuel could not turn God now. Jeremiah laments his birth; God promises to make him a bronze wall.
15.d: God answers that Judah’s destruction cannot now be avoided [[tosn:Jeremiah 15:1–9]]. The Tyndale dictionary suggests 15:16 may recall the finding of the lost Book of the Covenant under Josiah [[tbd:010:Jeremiah (Person)]].

16.s: Jeremiah is told not to marry, mourn or feast, as a sign. Yet God will one day bring Israel back from the north.
16.d: In Hebrew society men were expected to marry young, so Jeremiah’s single life was itself a sign of the crisis [[tosn:Jeremiah 16:1–2]]. God still planned to bring his people home from exile [[tosn:Jeremiah 16:14–15]].

17.s: Judah’s sin is engraved with a diamond point. Cursed is the one who trusts in man; blessed is the one who trusts God, like a tree by water. “The heart is deceitful above all things.”
17.d: The tree by the water echoes Psalm 1 [[tosn:Jeremiah 17:7–8]]. The people’s Baal worship is listed as the reason for judgement [[tosn:Jeremiah 17:1–4]].

18.s: At the potter’s house Jeremiah sees a spoiled pot reshaped: “As the clay in the potter’s hand, so are you in my hand.”
18.d: At the potter’s house God compares himself to a potter who may reshape or destroy what he makes [[tosn:Jeremiah 18:5–6]]. Paul uses the potter and clay in Romans 9:20–21 [[bible:Romans 9:20-21]].

19.s: Jeremiah smashes a clay jar in the Valley of Hinnom as a sign that God will break Jerusalem.
19.d: Another acted parable: the smashed jar shows Judah would be destroyed beyond repair [[tosn:Jeremiah 19:1–15]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 19:10–13]].

20.s: The priest Pashhur puts Jeremiah in the stocks. Jeremiah complains: “you have persuaded me… there is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones.”
20.d: Pashhur, head of the temple police, has Jeremiah beaten and put in stocks [[tosn:Jeremiah 20:1–2]]. Here Babylon is named as the invader for the first time [[tosn:Jeremiah 20:4–5]], and Jeremiah cannot stop speaking God’s word though he is mocked [[tosn:Jeremiah 20:8–9]].

21.s: King Zedekiah asks Jeremiah for help against Babylon; Jeremiah says God himself will fight against the city.
21.d: Set during the Babylonian siege of 588 BC [[tosn:Jeremiah 21:1–10]]. The choice of life meant surrender to Babylon; death meant the sword [[tosn:Jeremiah 21:8–10]].

22.s: A message to the kings: do justice and defend the poor. Shallum and Jehoiakim are condemned; “to know me” is to judge the cause of the poor.
22.d: Based on the Sinai covenant, this sets out the duties of Judah’s kings: if they keep them, David’s line continues [[tosn:Jeremiah 22:1–5]]. Justice for foreigners, orphans and widows is required (compare Micah 6:8) [[tosn:Jeremiah 22:3]].

23.s: Woe to shepherds who scatter the flock. God will raise up for David a righteous Branch: “Yahweh our righteousness.” False prophets are condemned.
23.d: Unlike the failed kings, the coming righteous Branch will reign wisely and justly [[tosn:Jeremiah 23:5]]; New Testament writers saw this fulfilled in Jesus [[bsn:Jeremiah 13:1–24:10]]. God’s word is like fire and a hammer against false prophecy [[tosn:Jeremiah 23:29]].

24.s: A vision of two baskets of figs: the good are the exiles, whom God will bring back; the bad are those who stay.
24.d: After the exile of 597 BC some said the good figs were those left behind; Jeremiah said the opposite [[tosn:Jeremiah 24:1–10]]. “They will be my people, and I will be their God” becomes a personal reality [[tosn:Jeremiah 24:7]].

25.s: Judah will serve Babylon seventy years, then Babylon will be punished. The nations must drink the cup of God’s wrath.
25.d: This is the first time a set length is given for the exile, seventy years, fulfilled either 605–538 BC or 586–515 BC [[tosn:Jeremiah 25:11]]. The cup of the wine of God’s anger reappears in Revelation 14:10 [[tosn:Jeremiah 25:15]].

26.s: Jeremiah’s temple sermon nearly gets him killed; elders recall that Micah prophesied the same and was spared.
26.d: Jeremiah is tried before the priests and prophets for saying the temple would be destroyed [[tosn:Jeremiah 26:1–24]]. Elders recalled the prophet Uriah, who had given the same message, and Ahikam protected Jeremiah [[tbd:010:Jeremiah (Person)]] [[bible:Jeremiah 26:20-24]].

27.s: Jeremiah wears a yoke and tells the kings to submit to Babylon.
27.d: Jeremiah wears a wooden yoke as he gives God’s message to envoys of the nearby nations [[tosn:Jeremiah 27:1–22]].

28.s: The prophet Hananiah breaks Jeremiah’s yoke and promises freedom in two years; Jeremiah says he will die within the year, and he does.
28.d: The false prophet Hananiah publicly challenges Jeremiah in the temple, and only Jeremiah’s word comes true [[tosn:Jeremiah 28:1–17]].

29.s: Jeremiah writes to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, “seek the peace of the city”. “I know the thoughts that I think toward you… to give you hope and a future.”
29.d: A letter to the exiles taken in 597 BC [[tosn:Jeremiah 29:1–23]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 29:2]]. The seventy years were not new, but now the exiles had to accept them [[tosn:Jeremiah 29:10]].

30.s: A promise of restoration: God will restore the fortunes of Israel and Judah and heal their wounds.
30.d: Chapters 30–33 are often called “The Book of Consolation”, full of hope for restoration [[tosn:Jeremiah 30:1–33.26]]. The returns from exile came in 538, 458 and 445 BC [[tosn:Jeremiah 30:3]].

31.s: “I have loved you with an everlasting love.” Rachel weeps for her children. God will make a new covenant: “I will put my law in their inward parts, and I will write it in their heart.”
31.d: Matthew 2:18 applies Rachel’s weeping to the killing of Bethlehem’s boys [[tosn:Jeremiah 31:15]]. In the new covenant God writes his instructions on people’s hearts; it began with Jesus’ death [[tosn:Jeremiah 31:32–34]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 31:34]] [[bible:Hebrews 8:8-12]].

32.s: During the siege Jeremiah buys a field as a sign that “houses and fields and vineyards will yet again be bought in this land.”
32.d: Land would be nearly worthless after Jerusalem fell, so buying it was an act of hope [[tosn:Jeremiah 32:9–12]]. Matthew 27:9–10 may allude to this event [[tosn:Jeremiah 32:9–12]].

33.s: “Call to me, and I will answer you.” God promises a righteous Branch of David and an unbreakable covenant.
33.d: The nation’s hope lay not in avoiding destruction but in God’s plan beyond it [[tosn:Jeremiah 33:1–26]]. “Yahweh our righteousness” is a title for the Messiah (23:5–6) [[tosn:Jeremiah 33:16]], and the promise to David is as sure as day following night [[tosn:Jeremiah 33:19–22]].

34.s: Zedekiah frees Hebrew slaves, then the owners take them back; God condemns them.
34.d: God encourages Zedekiah, a weak and timid leader, with judgement and a promise [[tosn:Jeremiah 34:1–7]].

35.s: The Rechabites refuse wine out of loyalty to their ancestor’s command, a contrast with Judah’s disobedience.
35.d: The Rechabites obeyed their ancestor, while Israel rebelled against God [[tosn:Jeremiah 35:1–19]].

36.s: Baruch writes Jeremiah’s words on a scroll; King Jehoiakim cuts it up and burns it, and Jeremiah dictates it again.
36.d: In 605 BC, Jehoiakim’s fourth year, Nebuchadnezzar first attacked Jerusalem [[tosn:Jeremiah 36:1–2]]. Jeremiah dictated his messages to the scribe Baruch, who read them in the temple [[tosn:Jeremiah 36:4]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 36:8–9]].

37.s: During the siege Jeremiah is arrested as a deserter and imprisoned; Zedekiah asks him secretly for a word from God.
37.d: Zedekiah is a classic example of divided loyalty (James 1:6–8) [[tosn:Jeremiah 37:1–38.28]].

38.s: Jeremiah is thrown into a muddy cistern; the Ethiopian official Ebed-Melech rescues him.
38.d: Zedekiah lets officials throw Jeremiah into a muddy cistern [[tosn:Jeremiah 38:1–13]]; his rescuer, Ebed-Melech the Ethiopian, was not from Judah [[tosn:Jeremiah 38:7–8]].

39.s: Jerusalem falls in 586 BC. Zedekiah is blinded and taken to Babylon; Jeremiah is freed.
39.d: As Jeremiah had predicted, Jerusalem falls and Zedekiah is judged [[tosn:Jeremiah 39:1–10]] [[bible:2 Kings 25:1-21]].

40.s: Jeremiah chooses to stay with the poor in the land under the governor Gedaliah.
40.d: Gedaliah, grandson of Shaphan, governs from Mizpah, eight miles north of Jerusalem [[tosn:Jeremiah 40:6]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 40:7–12]].

41.s: Ishmael murders Gedaliah and many others.
41.d: Three months after Jerusalem fell, Ishmael murders Gedaliah at a shared meal [[tosn:Jeremiah 41:1–2]].

42.s: The survivors ask Jeremiah for guidance, promising to obey; God says to stay and not go to Egypt.
42.d: The survivors ask Jeremiah for guidance in a request that seems sincere [[tosn:Jeremiah 42:1–3]].

43.s: They refuse and go to Egypt, taking Jeremiah with them.
43.d: Johanan and the others break their promise and refuse God’s message [[tosn:Jeremiah 43:1–7]].

44.s: In Egypt the people worship the “queen of the sky”, saying things were better when they did.
44.d: The queen of the sky (often called the Queen of Heaven) was Ishtar or Astarte; the people believed worshipping her brought prosperity [[tosn:Jeremiah 44:17]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 44:18]].

45.s: A short word to Baruch: “Do you seek great things for yourself? Don’t seek them.” He will escape with his life.
45.d: Set in 605 BC, over twenty years earlier: God promises the weary Baruch his life [[tosn:Jeremiah 45:1–5]].

46.s: Oracles against Egypt, including its defeat at Carchemish in 605 BC.
46.d: Chapters 46–51 are messages to foreign nations, like Isaiah 13–23 and Ezekiel 25–32 [[tosn:Jeremiah 46:1–51.64]]. The Battle of Carchemish was crucial for Babylon’s rise [[tosn:Jeremiah 46:9–10]].

47.d: A message about the Philistine cities, destroyed in the Babylonian advance [[tosn:Jeremiah 47:1–7]]. “You sword of Yahweh, how long” may be the cry of the cities under attack [[tosn:Jeremiah 47:6]].

48.s: A long lament and oracle against Moab, ending with a promise to restore its fortunes.
48.d: Moab, descended from Lot, is judged next (compare Isaiah 15–16) [[tosn:Jeremiah 48:1–47]].

49.s: Oracles against Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Hazor and Elam, some with promises of restoration.
49.d: Ammon and Edom are judged [[tosn:Jeremiah 49:1–6]] [[tosn:Jeremiah 49:7–22]]. Edom was famous for its wise men [[tosn:Jeremiah 49:7–8]].

50.s: Babylon itself will fall to a nation from the north, and Israel will return seeking God.
50.d: The judgement on Babylon is the longest for any nation except Judah [[tosn:Jeremiah 50:1–51.64]]. Babylon fell to Persia under Cyrus in 539 BC [[tosn:Jeremiah 50:3]].

51.s: More on Babylon’s fall; Seraiah is to read the scroll in Babylon and throw it into the Euphrates.
51.d: The scroll thrown into the Euphrates pictures Babylon’s permanent fall [[tosn:Jeremiah 51:63–64]]. John draws on these messages against Babylon in Revelation 18 [[bsn:Jeremiah 50:1–51:64]].

52.s: A historical appendix on the fall of Jerusalem and the release of King Jehoiachin in Babylon.
52.d: This chapter retells 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, with some added details [[tosn:Jeremiah 52:1–34]]. Since 51:64 ends Jeremiah’s words and 52 reaches events long after, it is an editorial addition [[tbd:002:Book of Jeremiah]].
